chapters.title: Chapter 6: Behavioral Macroeconomics: Bubbles, Panics, and Policy at Scale

lessons.title: Bank Runs and Contagion: The Psychology of Systemic Panic

children.text: In September 2008, Lehman Brothers collapsed. Within days, banks worldwide grew reluctant to lend to each other even overnight, at any price. This wasn't because every bank suddenly believed every other bank was secretly insolvent. It was because nobody could quickly tell which ones might be, and the safest assumption, given the uncertainty, became to trust no one until proven otherwise. Chapter 3 showed how panic can spread among depositors of a single bank. This lesson is about the same logic jumping between entire institutions, a scale where the psychology gets genuinely harder to distinguish from rational caution.

body.text: Financial contagion isn't just one bank's panic getting bigger. It's the same self-fulfilling logic jumping between institutions that may have no direct connection to each other at all, once uncertainty about who is exposed to what makes it individually rational to withdraw trust from everyone rather than take the time to find out who actually deserves it.

children.text: Recap: Why a Single Bank Run Can Be Self-Fulfilling

Chapter 3 covered this in detail: because a bank lends out short-term deposits for the long term, it can't pay every depositor back at once, so if you believe enough other depositors are about to withdraw, your own rational best move is to withdraw too, regardless of the bank's actual solvency. This lesson takes that same mechanism and asks what happens when the thing people are uncertain about isn't a single bank's health, but an entire network of interconnected institutions.
Contagion: When Panic Jumps Between Institutions

markDefs.definition: The spread of financial distress from one institution to others, either because they share a genuine underlying risk exposure, or because uncertainty about who is exposed makes withdrawing trust from everyone the safest short-term response.

children.text: travels through two genuinely different channels, and telling them apart matters. Informational contagion is a legitimate, rational update: if Bank A fails because of heavy exposure to a specific troubled sector, and Bank B has similar exposure, becoming more worried about Bank B too is actual evidence-based reasoning, not panic. Pure panic contagion is different: counterparties can't quickly verify exactly who is and isn't exposed to what, so the safest short-term action becomes withdrawing funding from everyone, healthy institutions included, simply because sorting the sound from the unsound takes more time than the panic allows. This is George Akerlof's asymmetric information problem from Chapter 6's first lesson, playing out under acute time pressure: when you can't tell the healthy banks from the troubled ones quickly enough, the market can end up treating all of them as troubled.

cells: A genuine shared risk factor between institutions
Yes, a legitimate update based on real, shared exposure
Inability to quickly distinguish exposed from unexposed institutions
Yes for each individual actor, even though it can needlessly damage healthy institutions

children.text: 2008: When Banks Stopped Trusting Each Other

The 2008 global financial crisis is the clearest large-scale example of pure panic contagion. Lehman Brothers' collapse wasn't the direct cause of every other bank's problems, most had no meaningful direct exposure to Lehman itself. What froze was the interbank lending market: banks that would ordinarily lend each other money overnight, routinely and cheaply, suddenly demanded far higher rates or refused to lend at all, a stress widely tracked at the time through the widening gap between interbank borrowing rates and expected central bank rates. Central banks worldwide, including the US Federal Reserve, had to step in directly as lenders when banks stopped lending to each other, precisely the lender-of-last-resort role Chapter 3 previewed.
India's 2018 IL&FS Crisis: A Domestic Contagion Case Study

markDefs.definition: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services, a large Indian non-banking financial company (NBFC) whose September 2018 default on debt obligations triggered a broader liquidity crisis across India's NBFC sector.

children.text: India's own version of this played out in September 2018, when

, a large infrastructure financing NBFC, defaulted on its debt obligations. The direct default was one company's problem. What followed was contagion: mutual funds and banks, unable to quickly assess which other NBFCs shared IL&FS's specific exposure to long-gestation infrastructure lending funded by short-term borrowing, became broadly reluctant to lend to NBFCs generally, tightening liquidity across the entire sector, including firms with genuinely different, healthier balance sheets. The government intervened by superseding IL&FS's board through the National Company Law Tribunal in October 2018, installing a new board to manage an orderly resolution, an intervention aimed less at IL&FS alone than at containing the sector-wide contagion its default had triggered.

body.text: Notice the parallel: 2008's interbank freeze and 2018's NBFC liquidity squeeze both hit institutions with no direct exposure to the original failure, purely because lenders couldn't quickly separate the exposed from the unexposed. Contagion doesn't require every affected institution to share the original problem. It only requires everyone else being unable to prove, quickly enough, that they don't.

children.text: "Too Interconnected to Fail": India's D-SIB Framework

markDefs.definition: Domestic Systemically Important Bank: an RBI designation for banks whose failure would be disproportionately disruptive to the broader financial system due to their size and interconnectedness, requiring them to hold additional capital buffers.

children.text: Some institutions sit at the centre of so many other institutions' exposure that their failure would trigger contagion risk on a scale disproportionate to their own size. The RBI formally recognises this through its

framework, which has designated SBI, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank as systemically important, requiring them to hold additional capital buffers beyond what a smaller bank needs. This is a direct regulatory acknowledgment of the contagion mechanics in this lesson: it isn't only a bank's own balance sheet that matters, it's how much of the wider system's confidence would be shaken if that specific bank failed.

body.title: Informational contagion, or pure panic?
body.scenario: NBFC X defaults after revealing heavy exposure to long-term real estate lending funded by short-term commercial paper. NBFC Y has a nearly identical funding and lending model. NBFC Z, in the same broad sector, is funded almost entirely by long-term bonds with no short-term borrowing at all, and has no meaningful real estate exposure. All three see their commercial paper yields spike and new lending dry up within days of NBFC X's default.
body.prompt: Using the two contagion channels from this lesson, how should a risk analyst assess what's happening to Y versus Z?
body.modelAnswer:
1. NBFC Y's rising funding costs largely reflect informational contagion: sharing X's specific structural weakness, short-term funding of long-term, illiquid real estate loans, makes worry about Y a legitimate, evidence-based update, not mere panic.
2. NBFC Z's rising funding costs, given no shared exposure and a fundamentally different funding structure, are much harder to justify as informational contagion. This looks like pure panic contagion: lenders unable or unwilling to take the time to distinguish Z's genuinely different risk profile from X's, defaulting to caution toward the entire sector.
3. This distinction should change the analyst's recommendation directly: X and possibly Y may warrant real caution, but Z represents a potential opportunity, a fundamentally sound institution temporarily mispriced by sector-wide fear rather than by any problem of its own.
4. The analyst's job here is precisely what the panicked market isn't doing quickly enough: taking the time to verify which institutions actually share the underlying risk, rather than treating the entire sector as a single undifferentiated block.

body.title: Which crisis mechanism is this?
body.question: After a large default, lenders across a financial sector broadly cannot quickly determine which other institutions are genuinely exposed to the same underlying risk, so nearly all institutions in the sector see funding costs rise together, regardless of their actual individual exposure. Which concept from earlier in the course best explains why uncertainty itself, not just the original default, does economic damage here?
options: Asymmetric information, since lenders can't cheaply distinguish exposed institutions from unexposed ones
body.explanation: This is a direct application of asymmetric information, the problem Akerlof's Nobel-winning work addressed: when one side of a transaction can't verify quality quickly and cheaply, uncertainty itself becomes economically costly, spreading damage well beyond the institutions that actually share the underlying risk.

body.title: Name the designation
body.textWithBlank: The RBI designation for a bank whose failure would be disproportionately disruptive to the wider financial system, requiring extra capital buffers, is called a ___ bank.
body.explanation: D-SIB status is a direct regulatory response to contagion risk: it isn't just about one bank's own balance sheet, it's about how much confidence in the wider system would be shaken if that specific bank failed.

body.title: Why did the government install a new IL&FS board rather than let it fail outright?

children.text: IL&FS's own creditors and shareholders were only one part of the concern. The larger risk was contagion into the NBFC sector broadly, and from there into mutual funds and banks that had lent to NBFCs, a chain the government wanted to interrupt before it spread further, similar in spirit to why central banks stepped in as lenders of last resort in 2008 rather than letting the interbank freeze resolve itself. Superseding the board through the National Company Law Tribunal gave the new management team, led by a professional turnaround specialist, a structured legal process to resolve IL&FS's assets and liabilities in an orderly way, aimed at giving lenders and the wider market enough credible information to distinguish IL&FS's specific problem from the health of the sector overall, directly targeting the informational uncertainty that pure panic contagion feeds on.

body.label: The trigger for India's 2018 NBFC stress
body.context: IL&FS's default triggered sector-wide contagion in India's NBFC space, tightening liquidity even for NBFCs with no direct exposure to IL&FS's specific risks.

cards.definition: The spread of financial distress from one institution to others, through either genuine shared risk exposure or uncertainty-driven panic.
A legitimate, evidence-based update in confidence toward institutions genuinely sharing a failed institution's underlying risk exposure.
Withdrawing trust from an entire sector because sorting exposed from unexposed institutions can't happen quickly enough, damaging even healthy institutions.
India's September 2018 NBFC sector liquidity crisis, triggered by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services defaulting on its debt obligations.
An RBI designation, currently including SBI, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank, for banks whose failure would be disproportionately disruptive to the financial system, requiring extra capital buffers.

points: Financial contagion is Chapter 3's bank-run logic operating between institutions rather than within one, and it travels through two distinct channels: legitimate informational updates about shared risk, and pure panic driven by an inability to quickly tell exposed institutions from unexposed ones.

The 2008 global financial crisis's interbank lending freeze is a clear example of pure panic contagion: most banks had little direct exposure to Lehman Brothers, but couldn't quickly verify who did, so trust collapsed broadly.

India's 2018 IL&FS default triggered the same pattern domestically, tightening liquidity across NBFCs with genuinely different risk profiles from IL&FS itself, resolved partly through a government-led board supersession aimed at restoring credible information to the market.

RBI's D-SIB framework is a direct regulatory acknowledgment that some institutions' failure would trigger disproportionate contagion risk, requiring them to hold extra capital precisely because of how interconnected, not just how large, they are.

The final lesson of this course and this chapter turns to how central banks use exactly this understanding, of confidence, information, and contagion, as deliberate tools of monetary and financial stability policy.
